label: Coneybury Anomaly feasting pit: earliest cattle bone 3950-3790 BCE
note: English Heritage: the earliest cattle bone from the Stonehenge landscape, 3950-3790 BC, came from the Coneybury Anomaly, a feasting pit. That dates one bone, not every use of the pit; the tick is placed at the middle of the range.

label: Robin Hood's Ball and first long barrows
note: Approximate. Robin Hood's Ball (causewayed enclosure, outside this map) is dated 'centuries around 3500 BC' by English Heritage; Amesbury 42 long barrow gave 3640 to 3370 cal BCE. Most other long barrows are undated.

label: Greater Cursus built
note: A red deer antler in the west terminal ditch gave 3630 to 3375 BCE; a 2009 paper found another antler about a millennium younger, so the date is debated. Whether the Cursus or the Amesbury 42 barrow is older is unknown.

label: Stonehenge Stage 1: ditch, bank, Aubrey Holes
note: Darvill et al. 2012 Table 3 gives 3000 to 2620 BCE for Stage 1; the ditch itself is modelled at about 2955 to 2830 BCE (68%), and 2990 to 2755 BCE at 95%. The model switches it on in 3001 to 2995 BCE. The Aubrey Holes may predate the ditch.

label: Cremation burials at Stonehenge (c. 3000 to 2600 BCE)
note: More than 150 people were probably buried as cremations in the Aubrey Holes and ditch; the span is a range, not an event. One cremated woman beside Aubrey Hole 7 probably predates the ditch.

label: Stage 2 begins: trilithons, bluestone double circle
note: Start of Darvill et al.'s Stage 2 (2620 to 2480 BCE). Order within the stage is not settled: trilithons first, then sarsen circle, or all in quick succession.

label: Woodhenge timber rings raised (c. 2635-2575 BCE)
note: Historic England 2024 chronological model (95% range); the tick is a display year.

label: Sarsen circle raised (modelled c. 2560 to 2470 BCE)
note: The English Heritage Bayesian model puts the sarsen circle at 2580 to 2475 BCE and the trilithons at 2585 to 2400 BCE (93%). The span shown is a modelling choice inside those ranges.

label: Durrington Walls village
note: Eight houses excavated in 2006 about 5 m square, dated 2600 to 2500 BCE at first; later modelling gives an occupation of only about 10 to 12 years ending c. 2500 to 2460 BCE. The number of houses is unknown (a few dozen is shown, conjecturally).

label: Durrington timber ring replaced by the henge bank
note: About 300 posts in a ring 440 to 450 m across were pulled and the sockets packed with chalk; the henge bank and ditch were completed c. 2480 to 2450 BCE. Also the start of Stonehenge Stage 3 (2480 to 2280 BCE).

label: Woodhenge ditch and bank built (display date c. 2400 BCE)
note: Historic England's 2024 model: timber settings 2635-2575 cal BC; ditch and bank 2495-2180 cal BC (93%), most likely 2465-2345. 2400 BCE is a display date.

label: West Amesbury henge (Bluestonehenge): stones removed
note: Stone sockets for up to about 27 stones, removed 2469 to 2286 BCE; the ditch and bank are c. 2400 BCE. That the stones were bluestones that went to Stonehenge is suspected, not proven.

label: Beaker burials: Amesbury Archer and a Stonehenge ditch burial
note: The Amesbury Archer (c. 2340 to 2300 BCE, grave outside this map) and a Beaker burial in the Stonehenge ditch (2340 to 2195 BCE) are of similar date.

label: The Avenue is built
note: Darvill: 2430 to 2200 BCE; English Heritage: four antler picks date construction to 2345 to 2200 BCE. About 2.5 to 2.8 km long, its first 530 m or so straight on the solstice axis. -2315 is a recommended display date inside the ranges.

label: Bluestone circle and oval (Stage 4)
note: Stage 4 is 2280 to 2020 BCE: circle modelled at about 2165, oval about 2060 BCE. Around 80 bluestones were used in all; 43 survive as stones or stumps.

label: Bush Barrow burial (c. 1950 BCE)
note: A rich Early Bronze Age burial on Normanton Down with a gold lozenge plate. The date of about 1950 BCE is from Wikipedia; the other grave goods are not itemised in the research notes.

label: Z holes dug (date uncertain)
note: English Heritage's model gives 2020 to 1745 BCE; its web page says 1800 to 1500 BCE. The holes were filled with windblown sediment. Purpose unknown.

label: Y holes dug; carvings on the sarsens
note: Y holes 1630 to 1525 BCE (modelled). Axe and dagger carvings are dated 1750 to 1500 BCE. The last prehistoric structural change, with the stone settings ending 1630 to 1340 BCE.

label: Middle Bronze Age fields in the east
note: A 2015 to 2016 survey found early fields and enclosures in the eastern part of the World Heritage Site. The sources say only 'Middle Bronze Age'; the date shown is the brief's.

label: Vespasian's Camp hillfort (placeholder date)
note: Iron Age hillfort of about 14 ha above the Avon. No construction date was retrieved; c. 700 to 600 BCE is a placeholder. The name comes from Camden and is not Roman.

label: Roman coins and pottery at the stones (late 4th century)
note: Late 4th-century coins and pottery were found at Stonehenge; Darvill thinks some bluestones were broken or removed in Roman times, his view not shared by all. A Roman building lay near the Cuckoo Stone.

label: Execution burial at Stonehenge (600 to 690 CE)
note: A decapitated man aged 28 to 32 was buried inside the stones. One source disputes the range; 'second half of the 7th century' is the safer wording. Low confidence on the exact span.

label: Amesbury Abbey founded
note: A Benedictine house founded c. 979 by Queen Aelfthryth. Its buildings and site within Amesbury are not known from the sources read.

label: Domesday Book: Amblesberie, 111 households, eight mills
note: Amesbury already a crossing of the London to Exeter road.

label: Henry of Huntingdon names 'Stanenges' (c. 1130)
note: One of England's four wonders in his Historia Anglorum, the stones 'raised up like gates'. The date is approximate.

label: Geoffrey of Monmouth: Merlin and the Giants' Dance (c. 1136)
note: In the Historia Regum Britanniae Merlin moves the stones from Mount Killaraus in Ireland. A legend, not evidence of construction.

label: Amesbury refounded as a Fontevraud priory
note: The abbey was replaced by a priory of the Order of Fontevraud. The medieval buildings are not located in the sources read.

label: Hardyng: stones 'somwat bowand' (c. 1457)
note: Hardyng's Chronicle says the stones 'hang' and are somewhat bowed: the only medieval hint of leaning.

label: Amesbury Priory dissolved (1539 or 1540)
note: Sources conflict: the project brief says 1539, the Wikipedia Amesbury article says c. 1540. The estate passed to Edward Seymour, Earl of Hertford.

label: Lucas de Heere watercolour (1573 to 75)
note: The first view drawn on site. The date is a range; the accompanying text was not read.

label: Camden's Britannia describes Stonehenge (1586)
note: Three circles within a trench, some stones 28 feet high with lintels on top. 1586 is the first edition; later editions followed.

label: Inigo Jones surveys for James I; Buckingham digs
note: James I visited Wilton in 1620 and commissioned a survey (per Webb's 1655 publication); the same year the Duke of Buckingham made the first known excavation in the centre. Jones's plan is an idealised restoration, not a record.
